claim: Memory Grafting introduces frozen Engram memory tables: the grafted table W_mem is built offline from a donor model's hidden states and is explicitly not updated during recipient-model training, with only the recipient-side projection and gating parameters learned.
stance_target: The repo's premise that frozen Engram memory tables exist and remove memory parameters from the trainable set
scope_conditions: Memory Grafting recipient training, 0.92B and 2.8B scales
quoted_support: The table Wmem is not updated during recipient-model training; only the recipient-side projection and gating parameters are learned.

claim: Memory Grafting retains a trainable hash-based Engram table as a fallback for n-grams not covered by the frozen table, so the memory subsystem is only partially frozen and still carries trainable parameters.
stance_target: The stronger claim that Memory Grafting makes the entire memory subsystem non-trainable
quoted_support: Memory-hit positions use the frozen grafted memory, whereas memory-miss positions use the trainable Engram fallback.

claim: The frozen grafted memory is large in absolute terms: for a Qwen3.5-35B-A3B donor, the top-1M n-grams per order across 3 orders (3M entries per layer) at bf16 come to roughly 12 GB of frozen memory per grafted layer.
stance_target: How much storage frozen Engram tables actually consume
scope_conditions: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B grafting model, layers 8 and 24, top 1M n-grams per order for n=2,3,4
quoted_support: For each n-gram order, we select the top 1M most frequent n-grams and compute their frozen memory representations offline, yielding 3M entries per grafted layer. Each entry stores a hidden-state vector of the grafting model in bfloat16; for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, this corresponds to roughly 12 GB of frozen memory per layer.

claim: A 0.92B-trainable recipient model carries approximately 12B frozen grafting memory, offloaded, giving a ~13:1 ratio of frozen memory to trainable parameters.
stance_target: Whether frozen memory can dominate total parameter count while trainable count stays small
quoted_support: The model of Memory Grafting has 0.92B trainable parameters with approximately 12B frozen grafting memory offloaded.

claim: Memory Grafting's stated motivation is that Engram training efficiency declines once the memory module exceeds about 70% of total parameters, so learning the table from scratch does not scale.
stance_target: Why freezing the memory table is attractive for a compute-constrained training box
scope_conditions: Engram pre-training scaling observations cited by the Memory Grafting authors
quoted_support: The memory table is learned from scratch during pre-training, so scaling it increases the parameters need to be optimized. Empirically, training efficiency began to decline once the memory module accounts for more than 70% of total parameters.

claim: Memory Grafting improves average benchmark score from 51.95 (MoE) and 52.43 (vanilla Engram) to 53.86 in a 2.8B-total / 0.55B-activated recipient trained for 100B tokens, with matched trainable and activated parameters.
stance_target: Whether frozen memory delivers capability gains at fixed trainable-parameter budget
scope_conditions: 2.8B total / 0.55B activated MoE backbone, 100B tokens, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B donor, lm-evaluation-harness, 9 benchmarks
quoted_support: Memory Grafting is best on all nine benchmarks: the average improves from 51.95 for MoE and 52.43 for vanilla Engram to 53.86.

claim: At the ~1B-trainable scale, vanilla Engram actually underperforms the MoE baseline (45.03 vs 45.62), attributed to a limited embedding table causing more hash collisions, while Memory Grafting variants recover the loss.
stance_target: The assumption that Engram memory helps uniformly at small trainable-parameter budgets
quoted_support: We also observe that vanilla Engram underperforms the MoE baseline in this 1B-scale setting, with 45.03 versus 45.62. These may caused by the limited Engram embedding table in 0.9B model, which lead to more hash collisions.

claim: Memory Grafting's runtime overhead versus a plain MoE baseline is small: 0.92x training throughput, 0.95x inference throughput, and 0.97x inference memory.
stance_target: Whether frozen-memory training is cheap enough to run on modest hardware
quoted_support: Memory Grafting keeps the runtime cost close to the MoE baseline, reaching 0.92x training throughput and 0.95x inference throughput, while using 0.97x inference memory.

claim: Grafted memory capacity scales monotonically with table size: increasing from 30k to 300k to 3M entries improves the training loss curve throughout training.
stance_target: Whether more frozen memory is strictly better
scope_conditions: Memory Grafting ablation on grafted memory size
quoted_support: Increasing the memory size from 30k to 300k and further to 3M improves the loss curve throughout training, indicating a clear scaling trend: grafting more memory provides more useful exact-match contexts and improves the recipient model more strongly.

claim: Exact longest-match suffix lookup over the frozen table is O(1) in expectation with respect to memory-bank size under hash-map or trie indexing, and costs a constant number of suffix queries per token because max n-gram order is fixed.
stance_target: Whether frozen-table lookup latency is independent of table size
quoted_support: The exact lookup is independent of the total memory size in expectation under hash-map or trie-style indexing, and costs only a constant number of suffix queries per token because the maximum n-gram order is fixed.

claim: The frozen memory only covers high-frequency n-grams, so using it alone introduces a hit-token bias during training; the trainable Engram fallback is required to mitigate coverage bias.
scope_conditions: Memory Grafting ablation on grafting mechanisms
quoted_support: Since the frozen grafting memory is built only for high-frequency n-grams, it cannot cover all tokens through exact matching. Using only this memory may therefore introduce a hit-token bias during training: tokens with matched high-frequency contexts receive grafting signals, while unmatched or low-frequency contexts receive no external memory.

claim: The donor model's layer choice matters: hidden states are extracted from roughly 10% and 60% of donor depth (layers 8 and 24 for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, 4 and 18 for DeepSeek-V2-Lite, 4 and 28 for GLM-4.7-Flash), and the choice of donor and layer changes the loss delta.
stance_target: How sensitive frozen-memory quality is to the donor
quoted_support: To cover different representation levels of the grafting model, we extract hidden states from an early-to-middle layer and a deeper layer, approximately corresponding to 10% and 60% of the model depth.

claim: Memory Grafting cites the Engram paper's own offload figure as roughly 2% end-to-end inference throughput cost for a 100B-parameter memory on a 4B-dense backbone, confirming the two sources agree on the magnitude.
stance_target: Cross-source consistency of the Engram host-offload overhead number
quoted_support: Engram [5] uses deterministic hash-based addressing to support O(1) retrieval per token, and reports that offloading a 100B-parameter memory only costs around 2% end-to-end inference throughput on a 4B-dense backbone.

claim: Memory Grafting's experiments are all at 2.8B total or below, so the technique has not been demonstrated at the 7B-total scale the repo's experiment program assumes.
stance_target: Whether Memory Grafting evidence transfers to a 7B-total model
scope_conditions: Recipient scales tested: ~0.9B and ~2.8B total parameters
quoted_support: We implement two recipient model scales [48], with total parameters around 0.9B and 2.8B.
